newsitem.title: TURKEY: FEATURE-Turkish villagers battle against gold mine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Turkish villagers battle against gold mine.

text.p: The people of Bergama in western Turkey are sitting on a goldmine but to the frustration of an international mining company they want the precious metal to stay in the ground.
Residents near the town, famous in antiquity as Pergamon, are determined to halt a project that will use cyanide to extract gold, fearing it will poison their bountiful land and scare off tourists.
"We are very rich, but foreigners come to take our riches," mayor Sefa Taskin said, warning of conflict if the central government does not respond to passionate protests against the mine.
Taskin visited the European Parliament Greens group in Brussels recently to enlist their support in stopping the mine, which is scheduled to start production in November.

"If the state does not listen to the people they will have to put gendarmes all around the mine," he said from his office seven km (four miles) from the green, picturesque area where the mine is located.

The company Eurogold, which worked tenaciously from 1991 to win approval for their mine, has dismissed concerns, saying cyanide is used in most gold mines worldwide and presents no danger to flora or fauna.

They say the local council-orchestrated protests do not reflect the views of the government in Ankara, which gave final approval for the mine last March and sees it as the start of a potential gold industry in Turkey.
"The central government supports development of the mining sector. We are only a small part of that, but we are the first and we are an example," said Eurogold managing director Jack Testard.
A team of mining experts in Turkey has said it believes the project to be safe.
UNOFFICIAL REFERENDUM

Local campaigners remain unconvinced and, despite rejection of appeals to the Council of State, have sustained the protests. Male residents, stripped to their underwear, paraded through Bergama late last year to bring attention to their cause.

Local people fear losing their livelihood and the countryside's beauty to cyanide through the pollution of water and soil. Olive trees, grains and vegetables grow in abundance in the area, near the Aegean Sea.

An unofficial local referendum of just under 3,000 locals came out unanimously against the mine and in favour of protests, which gained momentum after around 2,500 olive trees were cut down to make way for the mine.
"If necessary we will declare war on them, we will take up our weapons," said Gunduz Tosun, a 37-year-old farmer from a nearby village.

No gold has yet been extracted but mechanical diggers have begun to shift earth at the site, which takes up four square km (1.54 square miles). The village of Ovacik is within a stone's throw of the mine and Eurogold has agreed to relocate those nearest the fence.

"We will set up our tents there. This will go to the death," said 45-year-old Muzaffer Duran outside a tea house in the square of another village, Camkoy, where a group gathered to express their opposition to the mine.
CRUSADING MAYOR

Taskin, who leads the local campaign, gained the reputation of a crusader a few years ago in a so far futile bid to recover the 2,200-year-old Altar of Zeus, taken to a Berlin museum over 100 years ago. The altar, also excavated with official approval, was erected in gratitude to the god Zeus after the victory of a local king over invading Gauls.

In the modern battle both parties seek intervention from officials above. The mining company wants senior officials to come and give a seal of approval, villagers want them to come and stop the project.
The environment ministry in Ankara has expressed concern about the local anger and is keen to defuse the dispute.
Chris Power, site manager at the Eurogold mine, says the issue is not ultimately motivated by environmental concerns and has been hijacked by the mayor's own political agenda.
"With the mine he found a new bandwagon and he has done a very good job of distorting the truth," he said.

The owners of the mine project are Eurogold Madencilik A.S., a local joint venture two-thirds owned by an Australian-French venture controlled by Normandy Mining Ltd and one-third owned by Canada's Inmet Mining Corp.
LIVING WITH THE OPPOSITION
Eurogold, which had to obtain approval from 11 ministries, acknowledges it could have done more to explain safety measures and is now looking for ways to reassure the villagers.

The company says it is using the latest technology, such as a detoxification circuit and a tailings dam lined with a geomembrane to prevent leaks. It has also agreed to rehabilitate the area after the planned eight years of mining, planting two to three times as many trees as were cut down.
Power said the local community would benefit economically from the mine and rejected complaints it would harm tourism, saying tours of the mine could be organised.

Local people are among around 240 to be employed on the project, which is costing around $35 million to set up and will produce 110,000 ounces of gold a year after the scheduled start of production in November.

The majority of revenues from the mine will be kept in Turkey for further investment. Eurogold is planning a mine in the eastern Black Sea region and has sent a team to prospect other potential sites across the country.
